S2.F1.source_file: LibriTTS-VI: A Public Corpus and Novel Methods for Efficient Voice Impression Control
S2.F1.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the baseline (VIC-base) and the two proposed methods (VIC-sep and VIC-rfg).
citing_paragraphs:
For a fair and reproducible comparison, all systems are built upon a VITS backbone trained on the LibriTTS-R corpus [ 24 ] . For multi-speaker synthesis, the speaker encoder architecture is identical to that of the original VIC study, illustrated in Fig.  1 . It first processes a reference utterance 𝐫 \mathbf{r} with a speech encoder—composed of a pre-trained HuBERT [ 25 ] and a Bi-LSTM with attention—to generate an intermediate vector 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . This vector is then passed through a style token layer (STL) [ 10 ] to produce the speaker embedding 𝐠 \mathbf{g} , which globally conditions the modules within the VITS backbone, as in [ 5 ] .

After pre-training this backbone, we enable VI control by inserting a lightweight control module (CM) into the speaker encoder illustrated in Fig.  1 . We then finetune the module on our LibriTTS-VI dataset (detailed in Sec.  3 ). We evaluate three different variations of the CM: the baseline VIC-base, and our two proposed methods, VIC-sep and VIC-rfg, detailed in the following subsections.

The original VIC framework [ 23 ] provides an interface for VI control by inserting a CM into the speaker encoder before the STL, as shown in the left part of Fig.  1 . The CM processes information through two internal paths. One path accepts the target VI vector 𝐯 ∈ ℝ 11 \mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{11} , which is then processed by a linear layer. The other path takes the encoded reference audio 𝐱 \mathbf{x} (defined in Eq. ( 1 )) and applies a high-ratio dropout with a linear layer, followed by an adversarial VI learning module with a gradient reversal layer (GRL) [ 26 ] to extract speaker characteristics while removing the inherent VI. The outputs of these two paths are then concatenated, and a final linear layer projects the result back to the original dimension of 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , producing a modified vector 𝐱 ′ \mathbf{x^{\prime}} :

Our first proposed method, VIC-sep (“separate”), illustrated in the middle of Fig.  1 , aims to mitigate the impression leakage in VIC-base. We hypothesize that it is difficult to disentangle speaker identity and the target VI when both are sourced from a single utterance 𝐫 \mathbf{r} , even with dropout and GRL. To solve this, we introduce a second, separate utterance 𝐫 ′ \mathbf{r^{\prime}} from the same speaker, which replaces 𝐫 \mathbf{r} in Eq. ( 1 ). The original utterance 𝐫 \mathbf{r} remains the ground-truth synthesis target and the source for the target VI, thus decoupling the two information sources while keeping the model architecture identical to VIC-base.

Our second proposed method, VIC-rfg (“reference-free generation”), illustrated on the right of Fig.  1 , architecturally eliminates the impression leakage by removing the reference audio from the synthesis process. Inspired by the method for generating artificial speaker embeddings for voice privacy [ 19 ] , the speaker encoder is conditioned solely on the target VI vector. The encoded reference audio 𝐱 \mathbf{x} is then replaced with a random noise vector sampled from a standard Gaussian distribution. This method is therefore designed to strongly suppress the impression leakage from the reference audio. However, this architectural change introduced a challenge during training. We found that fine-tuning only the CM resulted in an unstable speaking rate. To stabilize it, we also jointly fine-tune the stochastic duration predictor (SDP) from the VITS backbone.

contextual_paragraphs.html: Fine-grained control over voice impressions (e.g., making a voice brighter or calmer) is a key frontier for creating more controllable text-to-speech. However, this nascent field faces two key challenges. The first is the problem of impression leakage, where the synthesized voice is undesirably influenced by the speaker’s reference audio, rather than the separately specified target impression, and the second is the lack of a public, annotated corpus. To mitigate impression leakage, we propose two methods: 1) a training strategy that separately uses an utterance for speaker identity and another utterance of the same speaker for target impression, and 2) a novel reference-free model that generates a speaker embedding solely from the target impression, achieving the benefits of improved robustness against the leakage and the convenience of reference-free generation. Objective and subjective evaluations demonstrate a significant improvement in controllability. Our best method reduced the mean squared error of 11-dimensional voice impression vectors from 0.61 to 0.41 objectively and from 1.15 to 0.92 subjectively, while maintaining high fidelity. To foster reproducible research, we introduce LibriTTS-VI, the first public voice impression dataset released with clear annotation standards, built upon the LibriTTS-R corpus.111The corpus and demo samples are publicly available at: https://github.com/sony/LibriTTS-VI

This paper addresses these two challenges to advance research in VIC. We propose two novel methods to mitigate impression leakage. The first is a training strategy for disentangling speaker and impression information, which uses two separate utterances from the same speaker; one to provide the speaker identity and another for the target VI. The second, inspired by the reference-free approach in [ 19 ] , generates pseudo speaker embeddings based solely on the target VI, providing both an architectural solution to the leakage and the practical advantages of synthesis without any reference audio. Our best method reduced the mean squared error (MSE) of 11-dimensional VI vectors from 0.61 to 0.41 objectively and from 1.15 to 0.92 subjectively, while maintaining high synthesis quality. Moreover, to promote reproducibility, we introduce LibriTTS-VI, the first public VI corpus built upon the LibriTTS-R dataset [ 24 ] .

This section details the systems used in our study. We first describe the VITS-based backbone TTS model [ 3 ] , which serves as the base model for all systems in this paper. We then introduce our baseline system, VIC-base, which is a reimplementation of the original VIC framework [ 23 ] . Finally, we present our two novel methods, VIC-sep and VIC-rfg, designed to improve upon the baseline.

Our baseline, VIC-base, is a reimplementation of this original VIC framework, replacing its FastSpeech2 architecture [ 2 ] with VITS for its superior audio quality. In our preliminary experiments, we observed some impression leakage from the reference audio, suggesting that dropout and GRL are insufficient to disentangle the inherent impression from the speaker characteristics.

The full results are listed in Table 4 . All systems achieved high speech intelligibility (CERs/WERs) and audio quality (UTMOS), confirming that our methods do not degrade synthesis quality. For speaker similarity (SECS), the reference-based VIC-base and VIC-sep achieved high scores (0.84 and 0.82). On the other hand, VIC-rfg’s score was noticeably lower (0.76), reflecting the expected trade-off of its reference-free design in reconstructing speaker identity. Next, we analyzed VI controllability and impression leakage. While the VI-MSE scores show only a slight improvement in control precision for the proposed methods (0.37 for VIC-sep, 0.36 for VIC-rfg) compared to the baseline (0.39), the impression leakage gap, Δ V \Delta_{\text{V}} , reveals a more significant difference. The baseline exhibits a large gap ( Δ V \Delta_{\text{V}} ) of 0.22. In contrast, our proposed methods narrow this gap to 0.14 for VIC-sep and a minimal 0.05 for VIC-rfg, demonstrating their superior robustness against impression leakage.

To further probe control precision, we conducted a modulation experiment, following [ 23 ] . For each of the 39 unseen speakers in the test-clean set, we modulated each VI dimension of an anchor VI vector from -3 to +3, synthesized 50 sentences per condition, and predicted the VI using our VIE. We then quantified the fidelity of VI control via the slope of the linear fit between target and predicted VIs, where a larger positive slope indicates more responsive control in the intended direction. As shown in Table 4 , while the slopes were generally mild, they were consistently positive for all dimensions except for E) Powerful-Weak, which was not learned effectively by any system. Among the systems, the average slope consistently increased from VIC-base (0.096) to VIC-sep (0.135), and finally to VIC-rfg (0.177), offering the most responsive control.

First, we conducted a controllability evaluation. For all three systems and both speakers, we selected 10 sentences for each of two conditions: single VI modulation (at levels -3 and +3) and the multiple VI modulation. We asked the same four annotators in Sec.  3 to rate the VI of the synthesized speech. Table  6 shows the MSE between the specified target VI vector and the scores provided by the annotators. While VIC-rfg struggled in the Mod. +3 setting for dimension I, the proposed methods generally outperformed the baseline in the single VI modulation conditions. In the challenging multiple VI condition, the proposed methods also demonstrated superior robustness, reducing the MSE from 1.15 for the baseline to 1.04 for VIC-sep and 0.92 for VIC-rfg.

Second, we conducted a Mean Opinion Score (MOS) test for audio quality, where 30 native or native-level English speakers rated samples on a five-point scale (1: Bad – 5: Excellent). The experimental setup was similar to that of the preceding controllability test in Table  6 , but it also included the neutral modulation level (0) and used 12 sentences per condition. Each of the 30 participants rated all stimuli, resulting in 30 evaluations for each synthesized speech. The results (Table 6 ) reveal several key findings. In the single VI modulation conditions, the proposed methods showed no consistent trend of audio quality degradation compared to the baseline, with VIC-sep having five significant improvements versus four degradations, and VIC-rfg having four of each. Moreover, with no significant quality differences observed in the challenging multiple VI condition, we conclude that our proposed methods achieve high controllability while maintaining audio quality comparable to the baseline.

In this paper, we addressed two key challenges in VIC: the issue of impression leakage and the lack of a public corpus. To mitigate impression leakage, we proposed two novel methods: a training strategy using separate utterances for disentanglement, and a reference-free generation model that structurally eliminates the leakage. Our experiments showed that these methods improve controllability while maintaining high synthesis quality. For reproducible research, we introduced LibriTTS-VI, a new public corpus for VIC.
